However, the appearance and structure of fields change dramatically from crop to crop and throughout the year, and it can be difficult to select a crop row tracking method suitable to all the situations that an agricultural robot is likely to encounter. DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSION This paper demonstrates a method of visually identifying the offset of crop rows in agricultural fields using a learning algorithm to rapidly learn a model applicable to a specific field in a quick and practical way with minimal human input. Results demonstrate it is applicable to a wide variety of fields and crops, and is able to perform online guidance of a robot. Our method currently uses a one-off batch mode approach to training. Output Filtering To improve tracking performance, we also apply spatial and temporal post processing to the output of the SVM. The predicted offset signal depicted in Figure 3.f is idealised and in practice we observe a noisier signal as shown in Figure 4.a. This makes locating the crop rows by at the local minima of this signal quite error prone. In order to more accurately locate the crop rows, we combine neighbouring offset predictions together by performing a template match of the predicted offset signal with the idealised template shown in Figure 4.b using a Sum of Squares Differences (SSD) similarity measure. The error output from this template matching produces a cleaner SSD Error signal shown in Figure 4.c. Note that the phase of this signal is opposite to the predicted offset, so crop rows are now located at the maxima of the SSD Error signal, and acceptable locations for our robot’s wheels (mid-way between the crop rows) are located at the minima. To further reduce noise, we also apply temporal filtering to the SSD Error signal with a simple complimentary filter, taking into account frame-to-frame offsets. The filtered SSD Error is used to estimate the position of the crop rows and desired wheel location. chunks.text: Abstract— This paper describes a vision-based method of guiding autonomous vehicles within crop rows in agricultural fields where the crop rows are challenging to detect or their appearance is not known a-priori. The location of the crop rows is estimated with an SVM regression algorithm using colour, texture and 3D structure descriptors from a forward facing stereo camera pair. Our system rapidly learns a model online with minimal user input, and then uses this model to track crop rows. Results demonstrate our method is able to learn and track a wide variety of crops with an RMS error of less than 3cm. We also present online control results demonstrating our system autonomously steering a robot for 3km. I. INTRODUCTION Automation of agricultural processes such as seeding, weeding, fertilising and harvesting has a key role to play in increasing farm productivity as well as meeting rising demands in food production. A key proficiency for most autonomous robots will be accurately guiding robots to drive with their wheels between the crop rows. It is common for large agricultural vehicles to steer along pre-planned paths using precise Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) receivers. However, high-precision GNSS steering systems remain expensive, require real-time correction data as well as a precise map of crop row locations. This has encouraged a great deal of research into guiding agricultural vehicles and robots using local sensors such as cameras [1-12] which are low cost and can provide a rich source of information. Generating Training Data The SVM is trained in a semi-supervised manner using labelled and unlabelled data. For a new field, two parameters are manually specified indicating the initial offset of two adjacent crop rows in the first frame. While driving in the field, these offsets are automatically transferred to subsequent frames using the frame-to-frame tracker (see Section III.A). This frame-to-frame tracker has very slow drift, usually less than 0.2% of the distance travelled, which allows the manually specified offsets from the first frame to be transferred to subsequent frames for a significant distance while still producing reasonable training examples. After training, the learned model is used to predict the crop row locations for the remainder of the run as well as for other rows within the same field. We generate training examples for the SVM with the same sliding window approach used at test time so as to generate multiple training examples with varying offsets for each training image. IV. Abstract— This paper describes a vision-based method of guiding autonomous vehicles within crop rows in agricultural fields where the crop rows are challenging to detect or their appearance is not known a-priori. The location of the crop rows is estimated with an SVM regression algorithm using colour, texture and 3D structure descriptors from a forward facing stereo camera pair. Our system rapidly learns a model online with minimal user input, and then uses this model to track crop rows. Results demonstrate our method is able to learn and track a wide variety of crops with an RMS error of less than 3cm. We also present online control results demonstrating our system autonomously steering a robot for 3km. I. A key proficiency for most autonomous robots will be accurately guiding robots to drive with their wheels between the crop rows. It is common for large agricultural vehicles to steer along pre-planned paths using precise Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) receivers. However, high-precision GNSS steering systems remain expensive, require real-time correction data as well as a precise map of crop row locations. Our system rapidly learns a model online with minimal user input, and then uses this model to track crop rows. Results demonstrate our method is able to learn and track a wide variety of crops with an RMS error of less than 3cm. A key proficiency for most autonomous robots will be accurately guiding robots to drive with their wheels between the crop rows. It is common for large agricultural vehicles to steer along pre-planned paths using precise Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) receivers. The predicted offset signal depicted in Figure 3.f is idealised and in practice we observe a noisier signal as shown in Figure 4.a. chunks.text: Abstract— This paper describes a vision-based method of guiding autonomous vehicles within crop rows in agricultural fields where the crop rows are challenging to detect or their appearance is not known a-priori. The location of the crop rows is estimated with an SVM regression algorithm using colour, texture and 3D structure descriptors from a forward facing stereo camera pair. Our system rapidly learns a model online with minimal user input, and then uses this model to track crop rows. Results demonstrate our method is able to learn and track a wide variety of crops with an RMS error of less than 3cm. We also present online control results demonstrating our system autonomously steering a robot for 3km. I. INTRODUCTION Automation of agricultural processes such as seeding, weeding, fertilising and harvesting has a key role to play in increasing farm productivity as well as meeting rising demands in food production. DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSION This paper demonstrates a method of visually identifying the offset of crop rows in agricultural fields using a learning algorithm to rapidly learn a model applicable to a specific field in a quick and practical way with minimal human input.
